title: September Visa Bulletin Brings Biggest Family Green Card Advances in Years
excerpt: Family-sponsored final action dates jumped by up to 29 months, with India gaining in F2B and F3 — but employment-based categories froze and India EB-2 stays unavailable.
body:
• The State Department's September 2026 Visa Bulletin, released August 22, brings some of the largest forward movements in recent memory across family-sponsored green card categories.
  • F3 advanced about 29 months to October 22, 2014, and F2B about 20 months to August 22, 2019; F4 moved more than two years to October 22, 2011, though India F4 remains at November 1, 2006.
  • Employment-based categories were essentially frozen: India EB-2 stays unavailable, and the bulletin warns EB-1 India, EB-2, and EB-5 unreserved could retrogress before the fiscal year ends September 30.
  • For September, family-sponsored applicants use the Dates for Filing chart and employment-based applicants use the Final Action Dates chart.

Family green card lines jumped by years in the State Department's September 2026 Visa Bulletin, released August 22 — one of the largest one-month advances across the family-sponsored categories in recent memory. F3 (married sons and daughters of U.S. citizens) moved forward roughly 29 months to October 22, 2014, while F2B (unmarried adult sons and daughters of permanent residents) advanced about 20 months to August 22, 2019. F4 (siblings of adult U.S. citizens) moved more than two years, to October 22, 2011, for worldwide and China-mainland applicants.

F1 (unmarried adult sons and daughters of U.S. citizens) advanced about 13 months to January 22, 2020. F2A (spouses and minor children of permanent residents) advanced one month, to August 22, 2026, and remains current on the Dates for Filing chart. The fiscal year 2026 limit for family-sponsored preference immigrants is 226,000, against 186,317 for employment-based preference immigrants.

Why the dates suddenly moved

The State Department attributes the family-side movement to decreased immigrant visa issuance for nationals of certain countries under recent administration actions, which freed up visa numbers that were then reallocated to applicants from other countries. In other words, unused numbers rolled forward rather than being lost — a mechanical redistribution that produced the year's biggest family-category gains in a single bulletin.

The advances are not uniform. India and Mexico did not see the same movement in F4: India F4 holds at November 1, 2006, and Mexico F4 at April 8, 2001, reflecting per-country limits that keep those lines far longer. But Indians still benefited elsewhere — the F2B final action date for India moved from January 1, 2018, to August 22, 2019, and F3 for India advanced from May 15, 2012, to October 22, 2014.

Employment side frozen — and warnings for India

Employment-based categories were essentially frozen this month. Only EB-4 moved, advancing two months to December 15, 2022. India EB-2 remains listed as unavailable, and the bulletin warns that EB-1 India, EB-2, and EB-5 unreserved could retrogress or become unavailable before the fiscal year ends on September 30, 2026, if demand and visa use reach annual limits.

"Family-based applicants received the most positive news this month. Several categories moved significantly forward — the largest movements were in F3, which advanced more than 29 months, and F4, which advanced more than 25 months."

— Tran Flores Law, September 2026 bulletin analysis

What this means for Indian families

For the Indian diaspora, the September bulletin is a mixed picture that mirrors the broader divide in the U.S. immigration system. Family-sponsored applicants with priority dates stretching back into the mid-2010s may suddenly find themselves current — a development worth checking against this month's charts immediately, since visa numbers can be claimed quickly once dates advance. But the employment-based backlog that ensnares hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals did not budge, and the bulletin explicitly flags possible further retrogression for India EB categories before October.

USCIS has confirmed that for September, family-sponsored adjustment-of-status applicants must use the Dates for Filing chart, while employment-based applicants use the Final Action Dates chart. Filing on the wrong chart is a common and costly error: always verify which chart USCIS has designated for the month before submitting Form I-485.

What's next

September is the last month of the fiscal year, which makes this bulletin both generous and volatile — numbers that go unused now could be redistributed again in October when fiscal 2027 begins. Watch the October bulletin for whether the family-side advances hold and whether the threatened employment-based retrogressions for India materialize. Applicants whose priority dates are now current should move promptly: visa numbers are finite, and availability can shift with a single month's bulletin.
